steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

- Quasiequations vs. purely equational axiomatization; action lattices
- Inequality notation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Definition
  - action algebra (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, ←, →, *)
  - (A, ∨, •, 1, ←, →) residuated semilattice, sense of Ward and Dilworth
  - (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, *) Kleene algebra, sense of Dexter Kozen
  - i.e. any model of the joint theory of both classes
- Axiomatization
  - Kleene algebras axiomatized with quasiequations (implications between two or more equations) -> so are action algebras axiomatized directly this way
  - advantage: equivalent purely equational axiomatization
  - language extends naturally to action lattices: add meet operation
- Notation
  - a ≤ b abbreviates a ∨ b = b
  - axiomatize with inequalities, still purely equational when expanded
- Star axioms (on top of residuated semilattice equations)
  - 1 ∨ a*•a* ∨ a ≤ a*
  - a* ≤ (a ∨ b)*
  - (a → a)* ≤ a → a
- Meaning
  - first splits: 1 ≤ a*, a*•a* ≤ a*, a ≤ a*
  - reflexive: 1 ≤ a; transitive: a•a ≤ a (abstraction from binary relations)
  - a* reflexive, transitive, ≥ a
  - second: star monotone
  - third equivalently a•(a → a)* ≤ a; role as induction
  - together with residuated semilattice axioms: a* least reflexive transitive element ≥ a
  - so a* is reflexive transitive closure of a in every action algebra

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
An action algebra (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, ←, →, *) is an algebraic structure where (A, ∨, •, 1, ←, →) is a residuated semilattice in the sense of Ward and Dilworth, and (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, *) is a Kleene algebra in the sense of Dexter Kozen. In other words it is any model of the joint theory of both of these classes of algebras. Kleene algebras are axiomatized with quasiequations, which are implications between two or more equations, and so action algebras are too when they are axiomatized directly in this way. But action algebras have the advantage that they also have an equivalent axiomatization that is purely equational. The language of action algebras can be extended in a natural way to that of action lattices, by including a meet operation.

Below we write the inequality a ≤ b as an abbreviation for the equation a ∨ b = b. This lets us axiomatize the theory with inequalities and still have a purely equational axiomatization when the inequalities are expanded to equalities.

- Star axioms (on top of residuated semilattice equations)
  - 1 ∨ a*•a* ∨ a ≤ a*
  - a* ≤ (a ∨ b)*
  - (a → a)* ≤ a → a
- Meaning
  - first splits: 1 ≤ a*, a*•a* ≤ a*, a ≤ a*
  - reflexive: 1 ≤ a; transitive: a•a ≤ a (abstraction from binary relations)
  - a* reflexive, transitive, ≥ a
  - second: star monotone
  - third equivalently a•(a → a)* ≤ a; role as induction
  - together with residuated semilattice axioms: a* least reflexive transitive element ≥ a
  - so a* is reflexive transitive closure of a in every action algebra

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
An action algebra (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, ←, →, *) is an algebraic structure where (A, ∨, •, 1, ←, →) is a residuated semilattice in the sense of Ward and Dilworth, and (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, *) is a Kleene algebra in the sense of Dexter Kozen. In other words it is any model of the joint theory of both of these classes of algebras. Kleene algebras are axiomatized with quasiequations, which are implications between two or more equations, and so action algebras are too when they are axiomatized directly in this way. But action algebras have the advantage that they also have an equivalent axiomatization that is purely equational. The language of action algebras can be extended in a natural way to that of action lattices, by including a meet operation.

Below we write the inequality a ≤ b as an abbreviation for the equation a ∨ b = b. This lets us axiomatize the theory with inequalities and still have a purely equational axiomatization when the inequalities are expanded to equalities.

The equations that axiomatize action algebra are the ones for a residuated semilattice, together with the following equations for star.

1 ∨ a*•a* ∨ a ≤ a*

a* ≤ (a ∨ b)*

(a → a)* ≤ a → a

The first equation can be broken out into three equations, 1 ≤ a*, a*•a* ≤ a*, and a ≤ a*. We define a to be reflexive when 1 ≤ a and transitive when a•a ≤ a, by abstraction from binary relations. Then the first two of those equations force a* to be reflexive and transitive, and the third one forces a* to be greater or equal to a. The next axiom says that star is monotone. The last axiom can be written equivalently as a•(a → a)* ≤ a, and in this form its role as induction is more apparent. These two axioms together with the axioms for a residuated semilattice force a* to be the least reflexive transitive element of the semilattice of elements greater or equal to a. If we take that as the definition of the reflexive transitive closure of a, then for every element a of any action algebra, a* is the reflexive transitive closure of a.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
An action algebra (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, ←, →, *) is an algebraic structure such that (A, ∨, •, 1, ←, →) forms a residuated semilattice in the sense of Ward and Dilworth,[1] while (A, ∨, 0, •, 1, *) forms a Kleene algebra in the sense of Dexter Kozen.[2] That is, it is any model of the joint theory of both classes of algebras. Kleene algebras are axiomatized with quasiequations, that is, implications between two or more equations, and so are action algebras when they are axiomatized directly in this way. However, action algebras have the advantage of also having an equivalent axiomatization that is purely equational. The language of action algebras extends naturally to that of action lattices, namely by including a meet operation.[3]

In the following we write the inequality a ≤ b as an abbreviation for the equation a ∨ b = b. This allows us to axiomatize the theory using inequalities while still having a purely equational axiomatization when the inequalities are expanded to equalities.

The equations that axiomatize action algebra are the ones for a residuated semilattice, together with the following equations for star.

1 ∨ a*•a* ∨ a ≤ a*

a* ≤ (a ∨ b)*

(a → a)* ≤ a → a

The first equation can be broken out into three equations, 1 ≤ a*, a*•a* ≤ a*, and a ≤ a*. Defining a to be reflexive when 1 ≤ a and transitive when a•a ≤ a, by abstraction from binary relations, the first two of those equations force a* to be reflexive and transitive, while the third forces a* to be greater or equal to a. The next axiom asserts that star is monotone. The last axiom can equivalently be written as a•(a → a)* ≤ a, a form which makes its role as induction more apparent. These two axioms, in conjunction with the axioms for a residuated semilattice, force a* to be the least reflexive transitive element of the semilattice of elements greater or equal to a. Taking that as the definition of the reflexive transitive closure of a, we then have that for every element a of any action algebra, a* is the reflexive transitive closure of a.

References:
[1] Ward, Morgan, and Robert P. Dilworth (1939) "Residuated lattices," Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 45: 335–54. Reprinted in Bogart, K, Freese, R., and Kung, J., eds. (1990) The Dilworth Theorems: Selected Papers of R.P. Dilworth Basel: Birkhäuser.
[2] Kozen, Dexter. (1990). Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS). Springer-Verlag.
[3] Kozen, Dexter. (1994). Logic and information flow. MIT Press, Cambridge, MA.
